core_thesis.market_pain: Developers using Claude Code, Codex and Cursor can ship working features, but the sites, slides, images and videos they produce look ugly, and hand-written Skills cannot fix that. Anthropic's official Skill library is free and has 186k stars, but it is messy and uncurated, so there is nothing to pick up and use directly.
core_thesis.opportunity_arbitrage: The break is curation by finished work: the team first hand-crafts a beautiful finished piece (a site, a slide deck, a video), then packages its templates, scripts and instructions into a SKILL.md. A free library of 475 viral Opus 5.5 videos - original clip, remake and full prompt - drives traffic, while the paywall only blocks the full Skill package and updates, at near-zero marginal cost.

metrics.revenue_model: Monthly Subscription ($19.90/mo) + Yearly ($158/yr) + Lifetime ($249); Black Friday 50% off at $9.99/mo until 2026-11-30

pitfalls_to_avoid: Watch three things. First, the last 7 days averaged about $288 a day, down more than 40% from about $503 a day in the week of September 29 - do not project monthly income from the peak week. Second, Marc Lou's shout-out brought mostly developer onlookers; the founder himself said it produced no paid conversions. Third, Anthropic's free Skill library and rival SkillGild are both out there, so the selling point is curation and finished-work quality, not volume.
summary: Hand-craft beautiful finished work first, then sell the method as a Skill: 475 viral Opus 5.5 videos with originals, remakes and full prompts free to attract traffic, while a subscription unlocks the full Skill library. Stripe-verified revenue: $10,913 in 29 days.
title: Skillry: Design-Taste Agent Skills Library
verdict: It sells curation, not code: a free library pulls traffic and a subscription collects payment, and one person can run it - but the last 7 days' daily average is already down more than 40% from the peak, so do not extrapolate from the breakout week.

workflow_steps.deliverable: 1 vertical + 5 finished pieces + 1 competitor price list
workflow_steps.detail: Do not start with a full catalog. Pick one vertical you know best, such as OG images, landing pages or launch videos. Break down the best work in that vertical from the last 30 days on X / YouTube, hand-build 5 finished pieces first, then talk about selling a Skill.
workflow_steps.title: Pick one vertical and build 5 finished pieces first

workflow_steps.deliverable: 5 installable SKILL.md packages + a finished-work comparison page for each
workflow_steps.detail: Write each Skill in one fixed structure: show the finished image or video first, then the templates, scripts and step-by-step instructions, then how to change colors, copy and layout without breaking it. Every Skill must be run from scratch by Claude Code and its output placed next to the original; if it differs too much, fix the Skill, not the screenshot.
workflow_steps.title: Turn finished work into SKILL.md and run it end to end

workflow_steps.deliverable: Free video library live + Stripe subscription + affiliate page with the first sale
workflow_steps.detail: Publish the viral-video library (original, remake and prompt) completely free, in the main navigation. Let a single Skill be tried free, with no card and no trial timer; the full library, updates and new Skills go behind a subscription: $19.90/month, $158/year, $249 lifetime. Take payments with Stripe and offer 40% affiliate commission for 12 months, starting with AI tool directory owners.
workflow_steps.title: Free library for traffic, paywall only for the full package

workflow_steps.deliverable: First 10-50 paying subscribers + a weekly revenue review sheet
workflow_steps.detail: Launch from the founder's personal X account with how-to posts, keeping the brand account as support. List on 10-15 AI tool directories in English and Chinese. Every week, redo one hot product with your own Skill and label it clearly as an unofficial concept. Review weekly revenue as a daily average and do not extrapolate from the peak week.
workflow_steps.title: Cold start from the founder account and directory listings

core_thesis.market_pain: Indie developers buy a domain for every side project, but none of them has email. Google Workspace charges $7 per mailbox per month, so 100 mailboxes cost $700/month. DNS records (MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC) are the step everyone puts off, and forwarding to Gmail can receive mail but cannot reply as the domain.
core_thesis.opportunity_arbitrage: The break is to turn 'write DNS + create a mailbox + send mail' into one sentence: tell the agent, or run one command, and the records are written automatically at Cloudflare / Vercel / Porkbun, a real IMAP/SMTP mailbox is created, and mail goes out via Amazon SES. A $5 flat monthly price against $700/month per-mailbox pricing is itself the advertisement.

pitfalls_to_avoid: Watch three things. First, FranklyMail charges $9/year for unlimited mailboxes and domains, about 1/7 of Plainmail's price, so the price ceiling is low. Second, new accounts are limited to 50 sends a day and the product is positioned for mail between people, not newsletters or cold outreach - do not drift. Third, there is no revenue proof yet; $340-$1,090/month is a model built from user counts, not measured results.
summary: Every domain bought for a side project ends up with no email: Plainmail writes DNS, creates a real IMAP/SMTP mailbox and sends via Amazon SES from one sentence or one command, $5/month for 50 domains and 100 mailboxes. Live on Product Hunt since 2026-11-05.
title: Plainmail: Real Email on Every Domain for $5 Flat
verdict: The price is itself the advertisement: rivals charging per mailbox need $700 a month for 100 mailboxes, while this one charges $5 flat - but there is no revenue proof yet, and a $9/year rival is pressing the ceiling.

workflow_steps.deliverable: DNS records tested on 3 providers + a 1-page buyer profile
workflow_steps.detail: Search Product Hunt comments and X for complaints about email for every domain, and confirm the buyer is someone with 3+ domains, not one. Test one domain on each of Cloudflare, Vercel and Porkbun, from creating the mailbox to receiving the first reply, end to end.
workflow_steps.title: Verify automatic DNS writing before selling anything

workflow_steps.deliverable: Working email service + CLI/MCP entry + 50 sends/day limit
workflow_steps.detail: The minimum version does three things only: write DNS automatically, create an IMAP/SMTP mailbox, and send via SES. Do not build newsletters or cold outreach. Limit new accounts to 50 sends per day to prevent abuse. Offer a CLI and an MCP entry point so an agent can run 'plainmail add hello@domain' for the user.
workflow_steps.title: Build only receiving, sending and DNS

workflow_steps.deliverable: Stripe $5/month subscription with the first sale
workflow_steps.detail: Sell one price only: $5/month for 50 domains, 100 mailboxes and 25GB. Sign up with GitHub, cancel anytime. After Stripe fees of about 5% and about $30/month for hosting and SES, 80 users net about $340/month and 240 users net about $1,090/month. Do not copy per-mailbox pricing - that is the opponent you are beating.
workflow_steps.title: One price, first sale via Stripe

workflow_steps.deliverable: Product Hunt launch + a target of 80 paying users
workflow_steps.detail: Launch on Product Hunt with the price and the bundle in the headline. Post in indie developer communities asking how many domains people hold and how they receive mail today. Watch FranklyMail closely ($9/year, unlimited mailboxes and domains, about 1/7 of Plainmail's price); your selling points must be steadier SES deliverability, MCP/Claude integration and active maintenance, not price alone.
workflow_steps.title: Launch on Product Hunt and watch the cheap competitor

core_thesis.market_pain: Owners of old trucks want a small plastic part the factory stopped making long ago, such as a dashboard bracket, an ashtray cover or a cup holder. Dealers have no stock and used parts are hard to find, so owners have to improvise. Generic 3D-printed bestsellers have already collapsed in price, from about GBP 14 to about GBP 4.50.
core_thesis.opportunity_arbitrage: Only a narrow niche - one specific model, one specific year, one specific part, with exact fitment dimensions - holds its price. Listen in Facebook owner groups for the part owners keep asking about, make that one part, test-fit it on a real truck, then list it on Etsy. Printer hours cap output; to scale, add a printer or sell only the STL file, not one bestseller all year.

pitfalls_to_avoid: Watch four things. First, since June 2025 Etsy requires 3D-printed listings to be the seller's own original design; printing someone else's STL file and selling it gets delisted. Second, do not use heat- or UV-sensitive PLA inside vehicles. Third, do not touch safety parts and do not use brand trademarks. Fourth, the $30,062 annual figure is a seller-reported Reddit dashboard screenshot relayed second-hand, not audited, and a China/domestic port is unverified.
summary: Pick one discontinued plastic part for one old truck model: one model, one year, one part, and exact fitment is what holds the price. $25 per printed part earns about $20, $150 per fully wired unit earns about $60-65; the seller reports 683 orders and $30,062 in a year (seller-reported, unaudited).
title: Vintage Truck 3D-Printed Parts: One Model, One Part, One Etsy Niche
verdict: Only a narrow niche holds its price: generic 3D-printed bestsellers have already fallen from about GBP 14 to about GBP 4.50, while 'one model, one year, one part' keeps its margin - but printer hours are the ceiling, so scaling means adding machines or selling only the STL file.

workflow_steps.detail: Do not sell '3D printing on Etsy' in general. Pick one discontinued old model with a large owner base and an active community, such as the 1973-1987 Squarebody Chevrolet. Join its Facebook owner group and find the one part owners keep asking about - a cup holder, an ashtray panel or a dashboard clip - and commit to one.
workflow_steps.title: Pick one model and one part

workflow_steps.deliverable: 1 original CAD file + fitment-test photos or video
workflow_steps.detail: Learn CAD on YouTube and draw your own original interior part. Do not copy OEM parts, do not touch safety parts such as brakes, and do not use brand trademarks. Print in heat-resistant PETG, fit it on a real truck, and revise until it fits exactly. Since June 2025 Etsy requires 3D-printed listings to be the seller's own original design; printing someone else's STL file and selling it gets delisted.
workflow_steps.title: Draw your own CAD and test-fit before listing

workflow_steps.deliverable: Etsy listing + first 10 orders + a returns process
workflow_steps.detail: Sell the printed part alone for $25, about $20 profit; sell the fully built unit with screen and wiring adapter for $150, about $60-65 profit. Etsy fees run about 11-15% and filament costs $0.50-3 per part. A steady beginner with 1-2 printers, 6-12 months in, makes about $500-1,500/month. Get the returns process working before adding a printer.
workflow_steps.title: Printed part for traffic, full unit for profit

workflow_steps.deliverable: About 10 orders a week with repeat orders
workflow_steps.detail: The original seller ran zero ads for a year and posted only in specific Facebook groups, averaging about 10 sales a week. Copy that: post a fitment test and owner feedback in the group once a week, do not spam. List on eBay too, but do not count on it as the main channel. To scale, add one printer first, then consider selling only the STL file.
workflow_steps.title: Post only in owner groups, do not buy ads
